task: OceanBase 2026 add-on round (MiniVectorDB): lightweight vector database, plus the Agent Prompt learning material itself

material_scope.what_this_file_is: Learning evidence for the MiniVectorDB add-on task. It records the student's own prompts, the student's questions and corrections, and the measured results that the student asked for. It is not a design document.
provenance: Sessions S1 (MiniVectorDB implementation, 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-10) and S2 (2026-11-10, this material plus follow-up measurement passes on the committed code, including engine fa7f74aed and the branch head c5d9d44c9).
Student turns are copied verbatim from the chat records. Chinese prompts are kept in the original language; only local absolute paths and credentials were removed.
Agent turns are summaries of what the assistant answered in the same session, not transcripts.
Every entry in experiments[] was executed; nothing here is a plan. Unexecuted ideas are listed in limitations.
desensitization: No access token, password or credential appears in this file. The repository is referenced by public HTTPS URL, branch name and commit SHA only.
Screenshot attachments that the student uploaded are described in words instead of being reproduced, because the images contain a repository URL with an embedded token.
Local Windows paths were replaced by tool names or by the recorded commands.
material_scope.environment_note: The graded environment is the Docker image in this commit: python:3.11-slim with a two-stage build (g++ compiles minivectordb/fastscan.cpp into libfastscan.so), PYTHONUTF8=1, numpy==1.26.4, MVD_REQUIRE_FASTSCAN=1, Linux x86_64. The S2 measurements below were taken on Windows with CPython 3.14.0a5 and NumPy absent, which forces minivectordb's pure-Python fallback path (no libfastscan.so builds on this host); each experiment states which numbers are environment-dependent. e12 re-ran the engine fa7f74aed and e14 re-ran the branch head c5d9d44c9 under the same Windows environment.
material_scope.not_included: Hidden formal cases (29 - 20 published) were never seen; nothing here quotes or reconstructs them.

commit_chain.summary: feat(minivectordb): implement SQL vector database and stdio server (first version spoke a guessed MySQL wire protocol, minivectordb/mysql_wire.py 292 lines)
fix(minivectordb): atomic multi-row insert and protocol salt
perf(minivectordb): append insert WAL instead of full snapshots (engine.py +59/-11)
fix(minivectordb): atomic update and verification evidence
feat(minivectordb): switch to official JSONL protocol and pass public cases (deletes minivectordb/mysql_wire.py 292 lines, adds minivectordb/stdio_json.py 127 lines)

fix(minivectordb): hidden vector errors and official Docker evidence (sql.py parses NaN/Infinity as numbers so the storage layer rejects them; stdio_json.py remaps 1264 from invalid_vector to value_out_of_range)
perf(minivectordb): compact float32 vector storage (2 files, 22 insertions, 9 deletions; VECTOR columns become array('f'))
perf(minivectordb): reuse cached float32 row norms for exact L2 scans (Table._norms cleared on touch; einsum row norms; sqrt(maximum(norms - 2*(M@q) + q.q, 0)) avoids a per-query temporary matrix)
docs(minivectordb): record successful Linux Docker public validation (CI run 42797438284, ci-round2 77f9effb5)

perf(minivectordb): compile C++ fastscan for exact L2 top-k (two-stage Dockerfile compiles minivectordb/fastscan.cpp to libfastscan.so with g++ -O3 -march=native; MVD_REQUIRE_FASTSCAN=1 makes a missing library fail loudly; engine calls the native TopK when NumPy is present and falls back to Python otherwise)

conversations.student: The student asked whether the screenshots they had provided contained the tests and cases (u2), then ordered a check of the official repository and the official page (u3).
conversations.agent_before: The first implementation answered SQL over a guessed MySQL wire protocol with a READY text handshake, because the task statement only showed stdin/stdout and mentioned mysqltest-style cases.
conversations.finding: The official branch publishes mysqltest/manifest.json with 20 public cases, STDIO_PROTOCOL.md (one JSON object per line, a ready object, per-request ids, structured errors, shutdown) and protocol_check/. The guessed protocol was wrong and the whole transport layer had to be replaced.
conversations.action: commit 34180eb65 deletes minivectordb/mysql_wire.py (292 lines) and adds minivectordb/stdio_json.py (127 lines). The same commit updates README.md and this conversation.json.
conversations.retest: All 20 public cases then passed locally and, in CI run 42778867412, inside the built image.
conversations.evidence: The student's two questions are the trigger of this correction chain; without them the guessed protocol would have failed functional admission and scored 0 overall.

conversations.student: The student required the highest performance result to be preserved (u5) while the Agent Prompt material was being prepared.
conversations.agent: That constraint was turned into a rule for this session: read-only experiments and material edits, no engine change, no Dockerfile change. The measurements below were used to decide whether the newest commit was actually the best one, not to change it.
conversations.result: The A/B run showed 202846704 wins on memory (peak working set 32.19 MiB vs 75.42 MiB) and loses on write time (+16%) and on WAL bytes, which is the correct trade for a score that weights query time twice as much as write time and counts page cache inside M.
conversations.decision: Keep the compact-storage line. The branch later gained fa7f74aed (cached row norms, a pure query-path win measured by the other session) and 862f97123 (docs); the material commit does not touch minivectordb/ or the Dockerfile, so the performance line stays at the branch head.

conversations.student: The task text the student pasted demanded 真实、可核验的学习记录 and explicitly not 不要提交密钥, so the material had to contain locatable results rather than claims.
conversations.agent: Instead of restating S1 conclusions, the committed engine was re-instrumented and re-run in S2. Three variants of the same engine (715379566, 2bff6fc84, 202846704) were executed with the same shape and the same seed, and the official protocol was driven through a real subprocess.
conversations.finding_the_material_had_been_over_claim: The S1 text said NaN/Infinity/overflow were all rejected as invalid_vector. The S2 re-run shows that is only true for NaN and Infinity, and that overflow rejection depends on NumPy being installed, because array('f') stores 1e39 as inf silently. The claim in this version is narrowed accordingly.

experiments.interpretation: 20/20 public functional assertions pass, including BIGINT precision, Unicode ordering, float32 storage, filtered TopK, ties by primary key, rollback and restart recovery.

experiments.environment: GitHub Actions run 42778867412, container flags --read-only --network=none, 2 CPU, 2 GiB, 128 PIDs

experiments.purpose: Measure the official handshake and response shapes through a real subprocess of the committed code.
experiments.command: py -m minivectordb.main --data-dir <empty dir>, one JSON request per line on stdin
experiments.environment: Windows, CPython 3.14.0a5, NumPy absent (pure-Python fallback path)
experiments.output: first stdout line {"type":"ready"} ; INSERT of 2 rows -> {"id":2,"ok":true,"affected_rows":2} ; SELECT id, L2_DISTANCE(...) -> {"id":3,"ok":true,"columns":["id","d"],"rows":[[1,0.1414213562373095],[2,1.2727922061357855]]} ; shutdown -> {"id":4,"ok":true} with exit code 0. Nothing but JSON lines appears on stdout; minivectordb: ready goes to stderr.
experiments.interpretation: ready/execute/shutdown framing, id echo, columns+rows for queries and affected_rows for writes all match STDIO_PROTOCOL.md. Distances are float32 values (0.1414213562373095) so a 1e-5 comparison tolerance is required, which is what the official driver does.

experiments.purpose: A/B of the durability strategy at the benchmark shape: full snapshot per autocommit (715379566) vs append-only insert WAL (2bff6fc84).
experiments.hypothesis: Rewriting the whole JSON snapshot for every 100-row batch is O(n) per batch, so load time and written bytes should grow with the table; appending one WAL line per batch should be flat.
experiments.command: py probe.py <variant> 10000 128 100 <data dir>  (100 autocommitted batch INSERTs, process memory and write counters read with kernel32)
experiments.environment: Windows, CPython 3.14.0a5, NumPy absent; write bytes are the process WriteFile counters, not cgroup io.stat
experiments.output: snapshot-per-batch: t_load 116.709 s, io_write 599.02 MiB in 76688 write operations, final minivectordb.json 12437862 B, no WAL. append WAL: t_load 6.903 s, io_write 11.86 MiB in 201 write operations, minivectordb.json 278 B + minivectordb.wal 12440285 B in 100 lines.
experiments.interpretation: The append-only WAL (commit 36d3f9188) removed 16.9x of write time and 50x of written bytes at the 10,000 x 128 shape, and turned 76,688 write syscalls into 201. This is the reason write T and write B are no longer the bottleneck of this implementation.
experiments.follow_up: Because the WAL is folded back into a snapshot at the next startup, the recovery cost is one extra full write; e8 checks that this fold is idempotent.

experiments.purpose: Independent truth check of filtered TopK, ties, K larger than the matching set, ANN mode and index maintenance.
experiments.command: py proto_test.py (2000 x 128 vectors, 5 categories, 100-row batches; then 4 single queries + 20 mixed queries; brute force truth recomputed in the harness from struct.float32-rounded values)
experiments.environment: same as e4; the harness computes the expected answer itself, so it does not reuse engine code
experiments.output: load 1.89 s. unfiltered exact: n=10 pool=2000 recall=1.0 max_distance_err=2.1076869138880738e-08 sorted_asc=true. unfiltered with search_mode=ann: identical numbers. filtered c3: n=10 pool=400 recall=1.0 max_distance_err=2.1076869138880738e-08. 20 mixed queries: 2.56 s total. filter-then-TopK probe: rows 1 and 2 are the two globally nearest ones but carry category hot; WHERE c='cold' ORDER BY d LIMIT 1 returned [[3,7.0710678118654755]] (one row, not zero). ties: two vectors at distance 2.0 returned in primary key order [[9,2.0],[10,2.0]]. fewer matches than K: LIMIT 5 over 2 matching rows returned both. index maintenance: after CREATE VECTOR INDEX vi ON edge(v), an INSERT, an UPDATE and a DELETE, ORDER BY distance LIMIT 3 returned [[11,0.20000000298023224],[2,0.30000001192092896],[9,2.0]].
experiments.interpretation: Recall is 1.0 in exact and in ann mode because ann is served by an exact scan; the distance error is exactly float32 rounding (2.1e-8), so it stays inside the 1e-5 tolerance. Returning one row instead of zero for a filter that excludes the globally nearest rows proves the TopK is computed inside the filtered set rather than pruned afterwards.
experiments.limit: Recall 1.0 is a correctness statement, not a performance statement. An approximate index would be judged on larger data, which was not measured.

experiments.purpose: Enumerate the error surface through the protocol, on an empty table and on a loaded table.
experiments.command: py proto_test.py ; py proto_test2.py (18 statements against t(id BIGINT PK, v VECTOR(2), name VARCHAR(3)))
experiments.output: loaded table: NaN literal -> invalid_vector/vector element must be finite; Infinity and -Infinity -> invalid_vector; [1,2,3] and [1] -> dimension_mismatch; [1, abc] -> invalid_vector; duplicate pk -> duplicate_key; SELECT nope -> unknown_column; VARCHAR(3) with 5 bytes -> value_too_long; id 9223372036854775808 -> value_out_of_range; WHERE v = '[1,2]' -> unsupported_sql/vector comparison is not supported; UPDATE of the primary key -> unsupported_sql; ORDER BY nope -> unknown_column; L2_DISTANCE with one argument -> sql_error/L2_DISTANCE expects two arguments. 1e40 -> NO ERROR (accepted). empty table: SELECT nope FROM t -> ok with rows []; WHERE v = '[1,2]' -> ok with rows [].
experiments.interpretation: 17 of 18 statements answer with the documented code. Two real gaps were found by probing outside the public cases: validation of projected and predicate columns happens per row, so on an empty table an unknown column is not reported at all; and 1e40 is accepted because array('f') silently stores inf (see e9), which the image avoids only because NumPy is installed and _as_float32 checks np.isfinite. The previous version of this material claimed overflow rejection unconditionally; that claim was wrong for the fallback path and is corrected here.

experiments.purpose: Crash model: kill the process inside an open transaction, and after a commit, then restart on the same data directory.
experiments.command: py proto_test2.py / py proto_test.py (subprocess.kill(), relaunch with the same --data-dir)
experiments.output: BEGIN; DELETE FROM t WHERE id=1; then kill -> restart -> SELECT id -> [[1],[2]] (the delete did not survive). BEGIN; INSERT INTO t VALUES (77,...); COMMIT; then kill -> restart -> [[1],[2],[77]] (the confirmed commit survived). UPDATE then DELETE then a clean shutdown -> restart -> row 1 still carries [9.0,9.0] and row 2 is gone, data dir contains only minivectordb.json (219 B).
experiments.interpretation: Committed data survives a forced kill, uncommitted data never appears, and mutations that are not insert batches go through the atomic snapshot, matching the rule that a statement without a confirmed response must not partially apply.

experiments.purpose: Corrupt-recovery behaviour: torn last WAL line, and recovering twice.
experiments.command: py proto_test.py (kill after one batch, append a truncated JSON line to minivectordb.wal, start, shutdown, start again)
experiments.output: WAL before: 1 complete line (rows 1 and 2) plus an appended torn line for row 3. First recovery -> SELECT id -> [[1],[2]]. After the shutdown the directory holds only minivectordb.json (242 B). Second recovery -> [[1],[2]] again.
experiments.interpretation: A half-written line is skipped instead of failing startup, the replay is folded into a fresh snapshot, and re-recovering the folded snapshot is idempotent, which is what the requirement 在恢复途中再次终止 asks for.

experiments.purpose: Memory representation A/B at the benchmark shape and the mechanism behind the unexpected WAL growth.
experiments.hypothesis: If vectors are kept as Python lists of floats, each element costs a 24-byte object plus an 8-byte slot, so the row store should dominate peak memory for 10,000 x 128 float32 data; a compact float32 array should remove that.
experiments.command: py probe.py head 10000 128 100 ; py probe.py liststore 10000 128 100 (identical seed and identical SQL)
experiments.environment: Windows, CPython 3.14.0a5, NumPy absent. The absolute working set is CPython-on-Windows; the ratio between the two representations is what transfers.
experiments.output: list storage: vector_payload 39.6 MiB, peak working set 75.42 MiB, load delta 55.29 MiB, t_load 6.903 s, WAL 12440285 B. array('f') storage: vector_payload 5.76 MiB, peak working set 32.19 MiB, load delta 11.96 MiB, t_load 8.011 s, WAL 25724759 B. Mechanism probe: array('f') is serialized with tolist(), so 0.123456 becomes 0.12345600128173828 (19 characters) and -0.555555 becomes -0.555554986000061; struct.pack('f', 1e39) yields inf without raising.
experiments.interpretation: Compact float32 storage cuts the vector payload 6.9x and the peak container memory 2.3x, at the cost of +16% write time and a wider WAL, because a float32 value needs its shortest double round-trip text. Under the graded image the WAL width is the same for both representations, since NumPy rounding already widens the stored doubles; the memory win and the time cost stand either way.
experiments.trade_off: Against the published weights (write 1/3, query 2/3; inside each, time 60%, I/O 20%, memory 20%) a 2.3x memory gain plus a smaller page-cache footprint is worth 16% of write time, so the change was kept. This is also why no attempt was made to move back to lists.

experiments.purpose: Read-your-own-writes inside one transaction, including vector search, and a failed statement in the middle of a transaction.
experiments.output: table d: rows 1=[5,5] and 2=[6,6]; top-1 for '[0,0]' is [[1,7.0710678118654755]]. BEGIN; UPDATE d SET v='[0,0]' WHERE id=2 -> top-1 becomes [[2,0.0]]. DELETE id=1 -> [[2,0.0]]. INSERT id=3 -> ids [[2],[3]]. COMMIT -> [[2,0.0]]. Second transaction: BEGIN; UPDATE id=3 SET v='[0,0]' -> the tied pair resolves to [[2,0.0]]; ROLLBACK -> [[2,0.0]] with row 3 restored to [0.5,0.5]. Failed statement inside a transaction: INSERT with a 3-element vector into VECTOR(2) -> dimension_mismatch; the following INSERT of id=4 succeeds and COMMIT leaves [[1],[2],[4]].
experiments.interpretation: The transaction sees its own update immediately in the ordering result, an error in one statement does not remove the earlier statements' effects, and rollback restores both the visible set and the vector answer, which is the behaviour the 2.3 section requires.

experiments.purpose: Unicode and BIGINT semantics through the protocol.
experiments.environment: same as e4, child process started with PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8
experiments.output: INSERT of -9223372036854775808 and 9223372036854775807 round-trips exactly in SELECT id, and WHERE id = 9223372036854775807 returns that row. VARCHAR(4) accepts a 3-character CJK string and a 4-character ASCII string, and rejects a 5-character ASCII string with value_too_long. ORDER BY on the string column returns ASCII values before the CJK value, i.e. codepoint order. A first attempt at this experiment failed with UnicodeDecodeError because the child inherited the Windows ANSI codepage; PYTHONUTF8=1 in the image is what makes this a non-issue in the graded environment.
experiments.interpretation: Length counts Unicode codepoints, comparison is by codepoint, and 64-bit integers keep full precision because they never pass through a double.

experiments.purpose: Re-run the full measurement suite against the exact engine now at the branch head (fa7f74aed), after the branch gained the cached row norms change.
experiments.command: git archive fa7f74aed minivectordb; then py probe.py new 10000 128 100 <data dir> ; py proto_test.py ; py proto_test2.py ; py proto_test3.py
experiments.output: load: t_load 7.385 s, io_write 24.53 MiB in 201 write operations, minivectordb.json 278 B + minivectordb.wal 25724759 B in 100 lines, peak working set 31.98 MiB, vector payload 5.76 MiB. Retrieval: recall 1.0 in exact and in ann mode, filtered and unfiltered, max distance error 2.1076869138880738e-08; filter-then-TopK [[3,7.0710678118654755]]; ties [[9,2.0],[10,2.0]]; index maintenance [[11,0.20000000298023224],[2,0.30000001192092896],[9,2.0]]. Error surface: the same 17 of 18 codes as e6 and the same two gaps. Overflow probe: array('f') stores 1e39 as inf without raising; the NumPy range guard is present in _as_float32 and runs only when NumPy is installed.
experiments.interpretation: The norms-cache change (fa7f74aed) does not alter the load or storage path: every number matches the 202846704 run within run-to-run variance (t_load 7.385 vs 8.011 s). The change only shortens the NumPy query path, which this machine cannot exercise because NumPy is absent, so its query-speed effect is covered by e13 instead of being re-measured here.

experiments.purpose: Re-run the full measurement suite against the branch head c5d9d44c9 (the C++ fastscan engine), on the Python fallback path.
experiments.command: git archive c5d9d44c9 minivectordb; then py probe.py new 10000 128 100 <data dir> ; py proto_test.py ; py proto_test2.py ; py proto_test3.py
experiments.environment: same as e4; no libfastscan.so builds on this Windows host and NumPy is absent, so _FASTSCAN is None and the pure-Python path runs

experiments.purpose: Record the other session's evidence that the compiled fastscan library is really loaded in the graded Linux image, not merely built.
experiments.command: not re-run here; the other session's material records its own commands
experiments.environment: GitHub Actions ubuntu runner, docker build from the branch
experiments.output: CI run 42808556753: docker build, official handshake, all 20 public cases PASS, with MVD_REQUIRE_FASTSCAN=1 - the image aborts at startup if libfastscan.so cannot be loaded, so a green run proves the native path executed. Checked from this session: the public API reports conclusion success (status completed), and the run's branch commit 4c25a67d8 has the same object SHAs as c5d9d44c9 for Dockerfile, engine.py, fastscan.cpp, sql.py and stdio_json.py, so the tested engine is byte-identical to the branch engine.

retrospective: The first protocol guess (MySQL wire) was wrong. The student's question about missing tests led to STDIO_PROTOCOL.md and to replacing 292 lines with 127; reading the authoritative package is worth more than a plausible guess.

The public package is genuinely useful, but it is not complete: the two real gaps found here (column validation on an empty table, float32 overflow on the NumPy-free path) are outside all 20 public cases, so 20/20 green did not mean no admission risk.

Exact TopK is the safe core. It gives recall 1.0 for both exact and ann, satisfies filter-then-TopK and tie ordering with one code path, and costs latency on larger data where an approximate index would be ranked.

Keeping the row store as array('f') was the only measured change that traded write time (+16%) for memory (-2.3x). Deciding it against the published weights, rather than by taste, is what made it a keep instead of a revert.

The WAL is deliberately narrow: insert batches append, everything else rewrites a snapshot. That is fast for the benchmark load shape and simple to recover, but it makes UPDATE/DELETE on a very large table pay a full snapshot rewrite.
Re-running the previous material's own claims in a new session found an over-claim. Written evidence has to be reproducible, not inherited.

A follow-up session landed a norms-cache optimization on top of the measured storage change. Its load-path neutrality was re-verified here (e12), and its query-speed claim was attributed to its own measurement (e13) instead of being merged into this session's numbers.

The native fastscan follows the same discipline as every earlier optimization: a measurable improvement with the fallback preserved (e14), and a fail-loud environment guard (MVD_REQUIRE_FASTSCAN=1) so the graded image can never silently degrade to the slow path - the guard itself became the proof in CI (e15).
limitations: Only the 20 public cases were available. The hidden formal cases were never read, so the two gaps in e6 are risks, not failures that were observed on the platform.
ANN is answered by an exact scan. Small ann cases return exact results with recall 1.0, but no approximate index is implemented, so large-data ANN latency and recall ranking are unmeasured.
Data larger than the container memory budget is loaded into memory at startup; the 大于内存限额 scenario in 2.3 is not fully streamed.

The S2 measurements ran on Windows with CPython 3.14.0a5 and without NumPy, which forces the pure-Python math path, and the byte counters are process WriteFile counters rather than cgroup io.stat. Absolute times and absolute memory are therefore not comparable with the platform; the comparisons between two variants inside one run are.
Install of NumPy for the local run was attempted and did not complete, so the NumPy path was verified only in the image (e2) and not re-measured locally.
Write time and read time were measured on the same machine in the same process family but not in three rounds, so no median was taken; the platform runs three rounds per 3.3.2.

The 11.978 -> 9.885 s query sweep comes from the other session's local machine with NumPy installed; it was not reproduced on the S2 machine because the NumPy install there did not complete. CI run 42797438284 was verified from its public run page; its step logs require login.

The native fastscan path (c5d9d44c9) cannot be built on the S2 Windows host (no libfastscan.so, no NumPy), so only the Python fallback path was measured locally (e14); the native path rests on the other session's CI run 42808556753 (e15), whose engine was SHA-compared against the branch engine.
